name: com.clawhard/studio
title: Clawhard Studio
description: Token counts, contrast, time zones, cron, JSON, regex, EOL versions, DMARC, packages, Unicode, links

tools.name: tokendiet_count_tokens
tools.description: Use when the user asks how many tokens a text, prompt, log, document or code paste is, whether it fits a context window (128K, 200K, 1M), or how big something is before they send it to an AI. Returns the exact o200k token count (GPT-4o family and later; Claude and Gemini usually within about 15%), plus words, characters and how much of each window it uses. Counts are exact for that tokenizer. Example: {"text": "<the text to measure>"}. Not for shortening text.

text.description: The text to count (up to 200,000 characters).

tools.name: runsheet_create_schedule
tools.description: Use when the user wants a shareable run-of-show or day-of schedule for a wedding, conference, shoot or other event that guests or crew can open on their phone and that updates live when edited. Creates the page and returns a view link to share with everyone and a private edit link to keep. Start from a template (wedding, conf, shoot, blank) or pass your own items. Example: {"name": "Maya and Sam wedding", "date": "2026-09-12", "timezone": "America/New_York", "template": "wedding"} or {"name": "Offsite", "items": [{"time": "09:00", "title": "Welcome", "duration_minutes": 30}]}. Each call creates a new saved page.

timezone.description: IANA time zone, e.g. America/New_York. Default UTC.

template.description: Starter schedule. Ignored if items are given.

who.description: Vendors or roles on this slot

tools.name: halves_settle_up
tools.description: Use when the user shares a trip, dinner, household or group expense list and asks who owes whom, how to split costs, or how to settle up. Returns each person's paid, share and net balance, and the smallest set of payments that squares everyone up. Handles equal splits, splits among a subset, exact amounts and payments already made, with correct rounding. Nothing is saved. Example: {"people": ["Ana", "Ben", "Cy"], "expenses": [{"what": "Dinner", "amount": 90, "paid_by": "Ana"}, {"what": "Taxi", "amount": 24, "paid_by": "Ben", "split_between": ["Ben", "Cy"]}]}. Amounts are exact to the cent.

people.description: Names of everyone in the group (2 to 40, unique).

split_between.description: Who shared it. Default: everyone, equally.

exact.description: Optional exact amount per person (must add up to amount). Overrides split_between.

payments.description: Payments already made between people to settle up.

tools.name: halves_create_group_link
tools.description: Use when the user wants a shared place for a group (trip, flat, event) to keep adding expenses and see who owes whom, not just a one-time calculation. Creates a group and returns a link anyone can open without signing up to add and edit expenses. Anyone with the link can edit it, so share it only with the group. Each call creates a new saved group; halves_settle_up gives a one-off answer without saving anything. Example: {"name": "Lisbon trip", "currency": "EUR", "people": ["Ana", "Ben", "Cy"]}.

expenses.description: Optional starting expenses (up to 50), same shape as the settle tool.

tools.name: doorman_check_ai_bot_access
tools.description: Use when the user asks whether their site (or any public site), or a robots.txt they pasted, blocks ChatGPT, Claude, Google AI, Perplexity or other AI crawlers, whether AI can read or train on their content, or why AI search does not mention their site. Fetches the live robots.txt and reports, for 22 named AI bots in four groups (AI training, AI search, assistants, search engines), which are let in, kept out or partly blocked, plus the site's content-signal preference and fixes. Example: {"url": "example.com"} or {"robots_txt": "User-agent: GPTBot\nDisallow: /"}. Pass robots_txt instead of url to check a draft or pasted file without fetching anything. Read-only.

url.description: Website address or domain, e.g. nytimes.com. Send this or robots_txt.

robots_txt.description: robots.txt text to check instead of fetching a site (a draft or a pasted file, up to 512 KB). Empty means no robots.txt.

tools.name: swatch_check_contrast
tools.description: Use when the user asks whether a color combination is readable or accessible, passes WCAG AA or AAA, or has enough contrast (text on a background, button, badge, link color), or what a color is in another format. Returns the exact contrast ratio, pass or fail for normal text, large text and UI components at AA and AAA, the APCA lightness contrast and a plain note. Colors can be hex, rgb(), hsl() or CSS names. Example: {"foreground": "#777777", "background": "#ffffff"}. Also returns each color in hex, rgb, hsl and oklch with its nearest CSS name.

foreground.description: Text (or icon) color, e.g. "#767676" or "rgb(20 20 20)" or "tomato".

tools.name: swatch_fix_contrast
tools.description: Use when a color pair fails contrast and the user wants the smallest change that makes it pass, such as "make this gray text accessible without changing the look". Returns the closest text color on that background that reaches the target (AA, AAA, AA-large or ui), and separately the closest background, keeping the hue. Example: {"foreground": "#777777", "background": "#ffffff", "target": "AA"}. Returns already_passes if nothing needs to change.

tools.name: swatch_make_scale
tools.description: Use when the user asks for a palette, shades, tints, a design-token scale or a Tailwind-style 50 to 950 ramp from a brand color. Returns 11 steps that keep the hue, with the hex, contrast on white and on black, and the best text color for each step. Example: {"color": "#ff5a1f", "name": "brand"}.

name.description: Token name used in the CSS and Tailwind output. Default "brand".

tools.name: swatch_check_pairs
tools.description: Use when the user has a whole design system, theme or stylesheet and wants every text and background pair checked for accessibility in one go. Takes up to 50 pairs and returns the ratio and AA and AAA results for each, with a count of failures. Example: {"pairs": [{"foreground": "#777", "background": "#fff", "label": "muted text"}, {"foreground": "#fff", "background": "#ff5a1f", "label": "button"}]}.

label.description: Optional name, like "muted text on card".

tools.name: meridian_now
tools.description: Use when the user asks what time or date it is right now somewhere. Reads the server clock and returns the current time, date, UTC offset, abbreviation and daylight saving status for each place. Places can be cities ("Tokyo"), IANA zones ("Europe/Paris"), abbreviations ("PST") or "UTC+5:30".

places.description: Cities, IANA zones or abbreviations, e.g. ["London","Asia/Tokyo"].

tools.name: meridian_convert_time
tools.description: Use when you need to convert a specific wall-clock time from one place to others, for any date. It uses the real tz database, so daylight saving is right for that exact date (the US and Europe switch on different weeks), and it warns when the time does not exist (spring forward) or happens twice (fall back). Time accepts "15:00", "3:30pm", "noon", "now" or an ISO local time like 2026-11-05T15:00 (no Z). Date defaults to today in the source zone. Returns {input, utc, source:{...}, converted:[{place, zone, local, time_12h, date, utc_offset, abbreviation, day_note, hours_ahead_of_source}], warning?, summary, open_url}.

time.description: Local time in the source place, e.g. "15:00", "3:30pm", "noon", "now", "2026-11-05T15:00".

from.description: Source place or zone, e.g. "New York" or "America/New_York".

date.description: Optional date YYYY-MM-DD in the source zone. Default today.

tools.name: meridian_meeting_slots
tools.description: Use when you need to schedule a call across several places. Scans the day in 15-minute steps and ranks start times so the most people are inside working hours and nobody is at night, using each place's real offset and DST for that date. Returns up to 5 slots with each person's local start and end, and says plainly when no time works for everyone. Defaults: working hours 9 to 17, 60 minutes, date today in the first place.

places.description: Where each attendee is, e.g. ["San Francisco","London","Tokyo"].

date.description: Date YYYY-MM-DD, local to the first place. Default today.

duration_minutes.description: Meeting length in minutes, multiple of 15. Default 60.

count.description: How many slots to return, default 5.

tools.name: meridian_zone_info
tools.description: Use when you need to answer "what is the UTC offset of X", "does X observe daylight saving" and "when do the clocks change". Returns the current offset and abbreviation, whether the place observes DST, every clock change in the year with exact local before and after times, and the next change. Abbreviations like IST or CST are ambiguous, so the answer says which zone was used.

place.description: City, IANA zone or abbreviation, e.g. "London" or "America/Phoenix".

year.description: Year to list clock changes for. Default this year.

tools.name: mend_repair_json
tools.description: Use when JSON from an LLM, API, log, config or copy-paste fails to parse (JSON.parse error, "Unexpected token", "Expecting property name"), or the user pastes JSON with trailing commas, single quotes, unquoted keys, comments, Python True/False/None, NaN, missing commas or brackets, a ```json fence, text around it, or output that was cut off. Deterministic repair: returns valid, formatted JSON plus a list of every fix with line and column. Values are never rewritten, so big numbers, number formatting and key order stay exactly as written. If the text is already valid it says so. Up to 100,000 characters.

text.description: The broken JSON, or any text that contains JSON (a chat reply, a log line, a code block).

indent.description: Spaces per indent level in the output. Default 2. Use 0 for one minified line.

sort_keys.description: Sort object keys alphabetically. Default false (keep the original order).

tools.name: mend_outline_json
tools.description: Use when you are about to read a big JSON response, log or export into context, before loading it: returns a compact outline of the structure (keys, types, array lengths, one example per repeated shape) so you can plan a query without spending tokens on the whole document. Repairs the JSON first if needed. Follow with mend_query_json to pull only the values you need. Up to 100,000 characters.

max_depth.description: How many levels to expand. Default 4.

max_items.description: How many array items to show when items differ. Default 6.

tools.name: mend_query_json
tools.description: Use when you need specific fields from a JSON document without reading all of it: $.users[0].name, $.items[*].id, $.a.b[-1], $.list[1:3], $..email (recursive). Returns each match with its exact path, type and value. Repairs the JSON first if needed, so broken input still works. Up to 100,000 characters.

tools.name: deadbolt_check_supabase_access
tools.description: Use when you write, review or are about to apply Supabase / PostgreSQL migration SQL (CREATE TABLE, RLS, CREATE POLICY, GRANT, views, SECURITY DEFINER functions, storage buckets), or when a user asks whether their Supabase data is exposed, whether RLS is set up right, or why a query returns 42501 permission denied or no rows. Replays the SQL with real Postgres rules and returns, per table, what signed-out (anon) and signed-in (authenticated) users can SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (all rows, own rows, some rows, none, or denied for a missing grant), plus findings with severity and ready-to-run fix SQL: RLS off, policies written but RLS never enabled, using(true) writes, personal columns readable by anyone, views that bypass RLS, SECURITY DEFINER functions anyone can call, user_metadata in policies, public bucket listing, grants missing after the Oct 30 2026 default change. Also accepts the JSON produced by deadbolt_catalog_query for the live database. Deterministic; never connects to any database. Up to 200,000 characters.

sql.description: Migration SQL (one or many files concatenated, in order), or the single JSON value returned by the catalog query.

project_created_before_2026_10_30.description: Only for SQL input. true (default): the project grants new public tables to anon and authenticated automatically (projects created before Oct 30, 2026). false: new tables get no grants unless the SQL grants them (projects created on or after Oct 30, 2026).

tools.name: deadbolt_catalog_query
tools.description: Use when you need to check a live Supabase project rather than migration files: returns a read-only SQL query that reads table RLS settings, grants for anon and authenticated, policies, SECURITY DEFINER functions and storage buckets (never row data) and returns one JSON value. Run it with the user's Supabase SQL Editor or a Supabase MCP execute_sql tool, then pass the JSON to deadbolt_check_supabase_access.

tools.name: spill_scan_secrets
tools.description: Use when the user asks whether some text contains secrets, or before you paste, commit, share, log or send code, a .env file, a diff, config, logs, a stack trace or a prompt that might contain credentials, for example "did I leak a key in this?", "is this safe to post?" or "redact the secrets in this log". Detects 48 services by exact key format (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini/Google, Groq, xAI, OpenRouter, Stripe, Supabase, AWS, GitHub, GitLab, npm, PyPI, Slack, Discord, Twilio, SendGrid, Resend, Shopify, Cloudflare and more) plus PEM private keys, database URLs with passwords, JWTs, Authorization headers and high-entropy values in variables named like secret, token, api_key or password. It verifies what it can deterministically: GitHub token CRC32 checksums, JWT and Supabase key role and expiry (service_role vs anon), documented example keys and placeholders, and NEXT_PUBLIC_/VITE_/EXPO_PUBLIC_ variables that ship to every browser. Returns findings with severity (critical, high, medium, public, info), line and column, a masked preview (never the full secret), why it matters, the fix and the provider's revoke URL, plus a redacted copy with labels like [STRIPE_SECRET_KEY_1]. Text is processed in memory to answer and is not stored. Limits: format-based, so a random secret with a neutral name can be missed; it never tests keys against providers; up to 200,000 characters. The same scanner also runs entirely in the browser at https://spill.clawhard.com.

text.description: The text to scan: code, a diff, .env, config, logs, a stack trace, a chat or a prompt.

redact_public_keys.description: false (default): keep keys that are meant to be public (Stripe pk_, Supabase anon or publishable, Mapbox pk.) in the redacted copy so the code still runs. true: hide them too.

tools.name: stamp_check_email_domain
tools.description: Use when the user asks why their email goes to spam, whether their domain is set up to send email, or before they launch a newsletter, cold outreach, transactional email or a new sending service, e.g. "why are my emails going to spam?", "is my SPF/DKIM/DMARC right?", "do I meet Gmail and Yahoo's sender requirements?" or "I added SendGrid, did I break SPF?". Reads public DNS (DNS-over-HTTPS) and checks: SPF (exactly one record, every include followed and DNS lookups counted per RFC 7208 against the limit of 10, void lookups, loops, +all/?all, ptr), DMARC (RFC 7489 syntax, policy, pct, alignment, inherited from the parent domain, and whether an external report address authorized it), DKIM (17 common selectors plus any you pass; key type and RSA key size read from the key, revoked or broken keys), and MX (provider, null MX). Returns a grade A-F, a verdict, each check with status pass/warn/fail/info, whether the Gmail, Yahoo and Outlook.com sender rules are met, and copy-ready DNS records to fix problems (e.g. one merged SPF record, a starter DMARC record). DNS cannot list DKIM selectors, so when none of the common selectors is found the result says so and a known selector (the s= value in a DKIM-Signature header) can be passed in. Accepts a domain, an email address or a URL. Results are cached for 5 minutes; pass fresh=true right after the user changes DNS.

domain.description: The sending domain, e.g. mycompany.com. An email address (you@mycompany.com) or a URL also works.

dkim_selectors.description: Extra DKIM selectors to try besides the common ones, e.g. ["mxvault"]. Find it as s= in a DKIM-Signature header or in the provider's setup page.

fresh.description: true to skip the 5-minute cache, e.g. right after a DNS change.

tools.name: stamp_check_dns_record
tools.description: Use when you or the user are about to publish or edit an SPF, DMARC or DKIM TXT record, for example after writing a new SPF record that adds a sending service, or when the user pastes a record and asks "is this right?". Detects the record type. SPF: syntax per RFC 7208, every include and redirect followed live in DNS and counted against the 10-lookup limit, void lookups, loops, the final all; returns a lookup tree. DMARC: RFC 7489 tags and values (p, sp, pct, rua/ruf, adkim/aspf, fo). DKIM: key type and RSA key size read from the key, revoked (empty p=) or truncated keys. Returns valid true/false, errors, warnings and where to publish it. Pass domain so a/mx terms without a value can be resolved.

record.description: The TXT record value, e.g. "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all" or "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@mycompany.com". Quoted chunks ("..." "...") are joined.

domain.description: Optional: the domain the record is for, so SPF a and mx terms can be checked.

tools.name: tick_next_runs
tools.description: Use when you or the user just wrote a cron expression (GitHub Actions, Vercel cron, Cloudflare Cron Triggers, systemd, an agent schedule) and need its next fire times. Pass the expression and an IANA timezone (default UTC). Returns the next N runs as local wall times and UTC ISO, a plain-English field breakdown, and DST gap/fold warnings (spring-forward skips, fall-back double fires). Example: {"expression":"0 9 * * 1-5","timezone":"America/New_York","count":5}. Uses the tz database, so DST rules match the region and year. Not for converting a meeting time across cities (use Meridian) or for email DNS (use Stamp).

expression.description: Cron expression: 5 fields (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week) or 6 with seconds first. Also accepts @hourly, @daily, @weekly, @monthly, @yearly.

timezone.description: IANA timezone for local wall times, e.g. America/New_York. Default UTC.

count.description: How many next runs to return (1–20). Default 5.

from.description: Optional ISO datetime to start from (default now), e.g. 2026-03-07T12:00:00Z.

tools.name: tick_matches
tools.description: Use when you need a yes/no on whether a cron expression would fire at a specific instant in a timezone — for example before shipping a schedule that crosses a DST transition, or to verify a single expected fire. Example: {"expression":"0 9 * * 1-5","timezone":"America/New_York","at":"2026-11-06T14:00:00Z"}. Returns fires true/false, the local wall time of that instant, and DST notes if the local time is in a gap or fold.

expression.description: Cron expression (5 or 6 fields, or a nickname like @hourly).

tools.name: notary_check_packages
tools.description: Use when the user or an agent is about to install or import npm or PyPI packages: before npm install or pip install, when adding lines to package.json or requirements.txt, or when a package name came from an AI answer, a tutorial or memory and may be invented. Looks each name up in the live registry and returns whether it exists, the latest version, whether a pinned version exists, weekly downloads, first and last publish dates, deprecation or yanked status, install-time scripts, whether the name is one or two typed characters from a well-known package, and real similar packages when the name does not exist. Example: {"packages":[{"ecosystem":"npm","name":"@anthropic/mcp-client"},{"ecosystem":"pypi","name":"requests","version":"2.32.3"}]}. Up to 10 packages per call; versions must be exact, not ranges. Not a malware or vulnerability scan: "ok" means it exists and nothing looked wrong.

ecosystem.description: Which registry: npm (JavaScript, TypeScript, Node) or pypi (Python).

name.description: The package name only, e.g. left-pad, @types/node or requests. No version, extras (requests[security]), URL or path.

version.description: Optional: one exact version to verify, e.g. 4.17.21 (npm also accepts a dist-tag like latest). Not a range such as ^4.17.0.

tools.name: xray_scan_text
tools.description: Use when the user asks whether text, a prompt, a SKILL.md, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, README, MCP tool description, PR diff, email or web page hides anything, or before an agent follows, installs or merges instructions that came from someone else (signals: "hidden characters", "invisible unicode", "ASCII smuggling", "prompt injection in this file", "Trojan Source", "why does this string not match", "is this domain spelled with a Cyrillic letter"). Inspects every code point and returns a verdict (clean, suspicious, dangerous) with each finding's line, column, code points and Unicode names: Unicode tag characters (decoded back to the hidden ASCII message), variation-selector payloads (decoded bytes), bidirectional overrides and isolates, long zero-width runs, zero-width and other invisible characters, ANSI terminal escapes, control characters, words that mix Latin with Cyrillic or Greek look-alikes (with the Latin word they imitate, from Unicode confusables), whole look-alike words, styled math letters, unusual spaces, line separators, private-use and unassigned code points, and HTML comments that do not render. Legitimate uses are not flagged (emoji ZWJ sequences, flag tag sequences, a single emoji variation selector, joiners in Arabic and Indic text, direction marks next to Hebrew or Arabic). Give text or url (one public https text file; GitHub and GitLab file pages are read as raw). Example: {"url":"https://github.com/owner/repo/blob/main/SKILL.md"} or {"text":"Visit pаypal.com","return_clean":true}. Optional return_clean adds a copy with hidden characters removed and look-alike letters inside mixed words replaced. Decoded hidden text is returned as data. Limits: finds characters and look-alikes, not prompt injection written in plain visible words; up to 200,000 characters (files up to 1 MB, first 200,000 characters scanned).

text.description: The text to inspect: a prompt, rules file, skill, README, diff, code, email or tool description. Give text or url, not both.

url.description: A public https address of one text file (raw file, GitHub or GitLab file page, Markdown, JSON, YAML, code or HTML source). Give text or url, not both.

return_clean.description: true: also return clean_text with hidden characters removed, unusual spaces made normal and look-alike letters inside mixed-script words replaced. Default false.

tools.name: vouch_check_links
tools.description: Use when the user asks whether links work, or before links, sources or doc URLs go into an answer, README, report, email or code comment (signals: "are these links dead", "check the links in this README", "does this URL exist", "404", "broken link", "where does this redirect", "is this docs page still there"). Fetches each URL live (GET, redirects followed hop by hop) and returns per link a status: ok, redirected (link the final_url), soft_404 (answers 200 but the title says not found, or a deep link lands on the front page), anchor_missing (the #section id is not on the page), broken (404, 410 or other 4xx), server_error (5xx), blocked (401, 403, 429 or a bot challenge: not proof the page is missing), unreachable (DNS, connection or timeout) or invalid. Each result has http_status, every hop, final_url, page title and canonical; for broken pages it lists the closest real pages from the site's own sitemap (suggestions, the top one re-checked). Give urls (up to 15) or text (Markdown, HTML or plain text; its http and https links are extracted, first 15 checked). Example: {"urls":["https://docs.stripe.com/api/charge","https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/a#attributes"]}. Limits: a page can work in a browser and still be blocked here; pages built by JavaScript may hide anchors; one call makes at most 45 requests.

urls.description: Up to 15 http or https addresses. A #fragment is checked as an anchor on the page. Give urls or text, not both.

text.description: Markdown, HTML or plain text (a README, an answer, a doc); every http/https link in it is extracted and the first 15 unique ones are checked. Give urls or text, not both.

suggest.description: true (default): for broken pages, look up the closest pages in the site's sitemap.xml. false: skip that lookup.

tools.name: vouch_check_quote
tools.description: Use when a quote, a statistic or a claim is attributed to a web page and the user asks whether the source says it, or before a citation goes into an answer, report, article or essay (signals: "does this article actually say", "verify this quote", "is this citation real", "check the source", "did they really write that", "fact-check this quote against the link"). Fetches the page once, extracts its visible text and returns per quote a verdict: exact (word for word), normalized (same words in order; only punctuation, capitals, spacing or curly quotes differ), close (similarity 0.85 or more, wording differs), partial (0.5 to 0.85) or not_found, with the matching passage, surrounding context, the words that differ and numbers_differ when a number changed (for example 1914 in the quote, 1912 on the page). Quotes with "..." are checked part by part. Example: {"url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Turing","quotes":["widely regarded as the father of theoretical computer science"]}. Limits: a match shows the words are on the page, not that the claim is true; pages built by JavaScript may have little text in their HTML; PDFs and paywalled or bot-blocked pages cannot be read; up to 10 quotes of 1000 characters, at least 3 words each.

url.description: The http or https address of the source page (an article, doc, blog post, Wikipedia page or plain-text file).

quotes.description: 1 to 10 quotes or claims to look for, as written in the draft (at least 3 words each).

tools.name: border_check_cors
tools.description: Use when the user hits a CORS error ("blocked by CORS policy", "No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header", "preflight", "Failed to fetch" from a frontend) or is about to call a public API from browser code (React, Next.js, Vue, a browser extension page) and asks whether it will work (signals: "CORS", "works in Postman but not in the browser", "preflight 401/404", "Access-Control-Allow-Headers", "withCredentials", "credentials include"). Sends the browser's own preflight (OPTIONS with Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method and -Headers) to the live API and, for GET and HEAD, the request itself with the Origin header, then applies the Fetch standard CORS rules as Chrome implements them. Returns verdict (allowed, blocked, preflight_passed, incomplete, same_origin, unreachable), the exact Chrome console error, which step fails (preflight or response) and why, whether a preflight is needed and why, the CORS headers the server sent, warnings (missing Vary: Origin, a server that echoes any origin with credentials, unreadable response headers, Authorization covered only by *), the exact response headers that fix it, and curl commands to reproduce. Example: {"url":"https://api.example.com/v1/items","origin":"http://localhost:3000","method":"POST","headers":["Content-Type: application/json","Authorization"],"credentials":true}. Limits: public http/https APIs on ports 80 and 443 only (localhost, private and staging servers go through border_check_cors_headers with pasted curl output); never sends POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE (those get the preflight checked only) and never sends header values for Authorization or keys; a server can answer differently to a real browser session.

url.description: The API address the page calls, for example "https://api.example.com/v1/items".

origin.description: The origin of the page that makes the request: scheme, host and port, for example "https://app.example.com" or "http://localhost:5173". A full page URL is reduced to its origin.

method.description: HTTP method the page uses (default GET), for example "POST", "PUT", "PATCH" or "DELETE".

headers.description: Request headers the page sets in fetch() or axios, as "Name" or "Name: value". Values matter only for Content-Type, Accept, Accept-Language, Content-Language and Range; give names alone for Authorization and API keys. Example: ["Content-Type: application/json","Authorization"].

credentials.description: true when the request sends cookies: fetch credentials: "include", XHR or axios withCredentials: true. Default false.

read_headers.description: Response headers the page code reads with response.headers.get(), for example ["X-Total-Count","ETag"]. Checked against Access-Control-Expose-Headers.

tools.name: border_check_cors_headers
tools.description: Use when a CORS problem involves a server Border cannot reach (localhost, a dev or staging server, a private network, a custom port) or a POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE whose real response needs checking, and the raw response headers are available from curl -i or the browser DevTools Network tab (signals: "here is the OPTIONS response", "my local API returns these headers", "CORS works on localhost but not in production", "preflight response is"). Parses the pasted OPTIONS response and/or the actual response (status line plus headers; curl -i, curl -v, curl -iL with redirects, and DevTools copies are all read) and applies the Fetch standard CORS rules as Chrome implements them, for the given page origin, method, request headers and credentials mode. Returns the same result as border_check_cors: verdict, the exact Chrome console error, the failing step and reason, warnings, the response headers that fix it, and the curl commands to capture any missing response. Nothing is fetched. Example: {"url":"http://localhost:8000/api/login","origin":"http://localhost:5173","method":"POST","headers":["Content-Type: application/json"],"credentials":true,"preflight_response":"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\nAccess-Control-Allow-Origin: *\nAccess-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type"}. Limits: the verdict is only as complete as the pasted headers; a preflighted request needs both pastes for a full answer.

url.description: The API address the page calls, for example "https://api.example.com/v1/items".

origin.description: The origin of the page that makes the request: scheme, host and port, for example "https://app.example.com" or "http://localhost:5173". A full page URL is reduced to its origin.

method.description: HTTP method the page uses (default GET), for example "POST", "PUT", "PATCH" or "DELETE".

headers.description: Request headers the page sets in fetch() or axios, as "Name" or "Name: value". Values matter only for Content-Type, Accept, Accept-Language, Content-Language and Range; give names alone for Authorization and API keys. Example: ["Content-Type: application/json","Authorization"].

credentials.description: true when the request sends cookies: fetch credentials: "include", XHR or axios withCredentials: true. Default false.

read_headers.description: Response headers the page code reads with response.headers.get(), for example ["X-Total-Count","ETag"]. Checked against Access-Control-Expose-Headers.

preflight_response.description: The raw OPTIONS (preflight) response: status line and headers, as printed by curl -i -X OPTIONS (see the curl.preflight command in any result) or copied from DevTools.

response.description: The raw response to the actual request: status line and headers from curl -i (curl -iL output with redirects is read hop by hop) or DevTools. Bodies are ignored.

tools.name: postcard_check_link_preview
tools.description: Use when the user asks how a link will look when shared, why a shared link shows no image or the wrong title, or wants a page checked before a launch post (signals: "link preview", "og:image not showing", "Twitter card", "X card", "social card", "share image", "unfurl", "Open Graph", "LinkedIn preview is blank", "after deploying the landing page"). Fetches the public page the way a link crawler does (following redirects, no JavaScript), reads the og: and twitter: tags with X's documented fallbacks (twitter:* then og:*, last twitter:card wins), downloads the og:image and twitter:image and reads their real pixel size, format and file size from the bytes, and checks robots.txt for Twitterbot and facebookexternalhit on the page and the image. Returns the card X, Facebook, LinkedIn and chat apps will build, every problem with severity and fix (relative or http image URL, image that is really an HTML page, SVG or AVIF, below X's 300x157 / Facebook's 200x200 / LinkedIn's 1200x627, over 5 MB, 2:1 crop of a square logo, tags added by JavaScript, tags past Facebook's first 1 MB, title over X's 70 characters, missing twitter:card, robots.txt blocks), and a paste-ready <meta> block. Rules come from the platforms' docs, with the check date. Example: {"url":"https://example.com/launch"}. Limits: public http/https pages on ports 80 and 443 (localhost and unpublished pages go through postcard_check_preview_tags); platforms cache cards (X for about 7 days), so a fixed page can still show the old card until rescraped; sites that serve different HTML to real crawlers by User-Agent can differ.

url.description: The page address people will share, for example "https://example.com/blog/launch".

tools.name: postcard_check_preview_tags
tools.description: Use when the share-card tags need checking in HTML that is not public yet: a page being built, a localhost or staging page, a template, or a <head> block the user pasted (signals: "check my meta tags", "are these og tags right", "before I deploy", "Next.js metadata", "index.html head"). Reads the og: and twitter: tags in the pasted HTML with X's documented fallbacks and returns the same result as postcard_check_link_preview: the card each platform will build, problems with fixes (missing og:image or twitter:card, relative image path, title over X's 70 characters, duplicates, name= instead of property=, tags in <body>, a JavaScript app shell with no tags) and a paste-ready <meta> block. The page is not fetched; with fetch_image true, a public absolute image URL is downloaded to read its real size, format and bytes. Example: {"html":"<head><meta property=\"og:title\" content=\"Launch\"><meta property=\"og:image\" content=\"/og.png\"></head>","url":"https://example.com/launch"}. Limits: robots.txt and redirects of the page are not checked (no fetch); without url, relative image paths cannot be resolved.

html.description: The page HTML, or at least its <head> with the meta tags (up to 400,000 characters).

url.description: Optional address the page will be served at, used to turn relative image paths into full URLs and to compare og:url.

fetch_image.description: true to download the public og:image / twitter:image and read its real pixel size, format and file size. Default false (nothing is fetched).

tools.name: stake_check_domains
tools.description: Use when the user asks whether a domain is available or taken, wants product, startup, app or project name ideas with a free domain, or is about to put a domain into a plan, README, config or launch post (signals: "is the .com taken", "domain available", "name ideas with a .com", "which of these names has a free domain", ".io or .ai", "who owns this domain", "when does it expire"). Asks each ending's own registry through RDAP (the official successor to WHOIS; IANA's server list plus the registries of .io, .me, .sh, .ac, .us, .so, .de, .ch that are not in it), and returns per domain: available, registered, registered_expiring (redemption or pending delete), likely_available (DNS only: for endings with no public RDAP such as .co, .gg, .eu, .it, or when a registry's RDAP server refuses or rate-limits the check), unknown or invalid; for taken names the registration and expiry dates, days to expiry, registrar, status codes and nameservers, and a flag when the nameservers belong to a parking or domain-marketplace service (Afternic, Dan.com, Sedo, Atom and others: the owner may sell it). Pass full domains, or names plus endings: {"names":["tidewell","brightloop"],"tlds":["com","io","ai"]} or {"domains":["tidewell.com","münchen.de","foo.co.uk"]}. Default endings when only names are given: com, io, ai, dev, app, co, net, org. Up to 20 domains per call. Call it before presenting name ideas as available instead of guessing. Cannot see prices, premium or reserved status, trademarks, or social handles; "available" is not a reservation.

domains.description: Full domain names to check, e.g. ["tidewell.com", "tidewell.io"]. International names (münchen.de) and suffixes such as co.uk are fine; a URL or subdomain is reduced to the registrable domain. Up to 20.

names.description: Bare names without an ending, e.g. ["tidewell"]; each is checked with every entry in tlds. Up to 10 names (and 20 domains in total).

tlds.description: Endings to try with names, e.g. ["com","io","ai","dev"] (a leading dot is fine; co.uk works). Default: com, io, ai, dev, app, co, net, org.

tools.name: jig_validate_json
tools.description: Use when the user asks whether some JSON matches a JSON Schema, or when JSON from a model reply, structured output, tool call, API response or file has to be checked against its schema before it is used or stored (signals: "validate this JSON", "does this match the schema", "which field is wrong", "the model returned bad JSON", "check the tool-call arguments", "why does my parser reject this"). Validates a JSON value (data), or raw model text (json_text: a ```json fence or prose around one JSON value is stripped; a syntax error comes back with line and column), against JSON Schema draft 2020-12, 2019-09, 07, 06 or 04, including $ref/$defs, anyOf/oneOf/allOf, if/then/else, unevaluatedProperties, patterns and formats (email, date-time, date, time, uuid, uri, hostname, ipv4, ipv6, duration). Returns valid true/false, every problem with its JSON Pointer path, keyword, expected and got values, and retry_message: a ready-to-send list of fixes for the model that produced the JSON. Example: {"schema":{"type":"object","properties":{"price":{"type":"number"}},"required":["price","sku"]},"data":{"price":"12.50"}}. Gives the expected answer on 6,018 of 6,227 official JSON-Schema-Test-Suite cases (ajv 8: 5,981); most misses are external $ref URLs, which are not fetched, $dynamicRef, and the idn-email, idn-hostname and iri formats, which are not checked. Not for repairing broken JSON syntax or for checking whether a schema works with OpenAI, Claude or Gemini (jig_check_schema).

schema.description: The JSON Schema, as a JSON object (not a string). $schema picks the draft; default 2020-12.

data.description: The JSON value to check: object, array, string, number, boolean or null. Use this or json_text.

json_text.description: Raw text that should contain one JSON value, for example a model reply. Code fences and text around the JSON are stripped. Use this or data.

draft.description: Force a draft: 2020-12, 2019-09, 7, 6 or 4. Default: from $schema, else 2020-12.

check_formats.description: Check "format" (email, date-time, uuid, uri, ...). Default true.

max_errors.description: Most errors to list (default 50). error_count is always the full count.

tools.name: jig_check_schema
tools.description: Use when the user asks whether a JSON Schema is valid, or whether it will work with OpenAI Structured Outputs or function calling with strict: true, Claude structured outputs or strict tool use, or Gemini structured output (response_json_schema), or is writing a tool or function schema, an MCP inputSchema, a response_format, or a schema exported from Zod or Pydantic (signals: "Invalid schema for response_format", "strict mode error", "Claude returns 400 for my schema", "will this schema work with OpenAI", "Gemini ignores maxLength", "additionalProperties false", "all fields must be required"). First checks the schema against its draft: type names like "int", "required": true on a property, misspelt keywords, unresolvable $ref, invalid regex, impossible ranges. Then checks each provider's documented rules: OpenAI (every property in required, additionalProperties false on every object, root an object and not anyOf, no allOf/not/if, at most 5000 properties, 10 levels, 1000 enum values, documented formats only), Claude (additionalProperties false, no minimum/maximum/multipleOf/minLength/maxLength, minItems only 0 or 1, no recursion, at most 24 optional and 16 union-typed parameters per request, regex without lookarounds or backreferences), Gemini (minLength, maxLength, uniqueItems, minProperties and similar are dropped without an error). Returns per provider a verdict (ok, warnings, fails), each issue with its JSON Pointer path, rule, fix and the provider's doc URL, plus a converted copy the provider accepts (optional fields made required and nullable for OpenAI, unsupported constraints moved into descriptions the way the official SDK helpers do), and counts (properties, depth, optional and union-typed parameters). Example: {"schema":{"type":"object","properties":{"city":{"type":"string","maxLength":40},"days":{"type":"integer","minimum":1}},"required":["city"]},"providers":["openai","anthropic"]}. Rules are from each provider's docs, checked 2026-11-18; providers can change them, and very large schemas can still hit unpublished size limits.

schema.description: The JSON Schema to check, as a JSON object (not a string).

providers.description: Which providers to check. Default: all three.

draft.description: Force a draft: 2020-12, 2019-09, 7, 6 or 4. Default: from $schema, else 2020-12.

include_converted.description: Include a converted copy for each provider that does not accept the schema as is. Default true.

tools.name: tack_check_workflow
tools.description:
Use when the user asks to write, review, fix or harden a GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/*.yml) or a composite action.yml, or when a workflow was just written or edited and is about to be committed (signals: "write a CI workflow", "why does my workflow fail", "Invalid workflow file", "Unexpected input", "pin actions to SHA", "is actions/checkout@v4 still current", "Node 20 deprecated", "upload-artifact v3", "runs-on ubuntu-20.04", "script injection", "pull_request_target"). Parses the YAML (errors with line and column, duplicate keys, anchors), checks the structure against GitHub's workflow syntax as documented on 2026-11-19 (including recent keys such as schedule timezone, cache-mode, background, wait, wait-all, cancel, parallel and $/ self-repository references), then resolves every uses: reference live on github.com: whether the repository, tag, branch or commit exists, which release a SHA is, the latest release, retired versions that make a job fail (upload/download-artifact v3 and older, actions/cache v1-v2 and old exact pins), runs.using node20-or-older runtimes, with: inputs the action does not declare (with a did-you-mean), missing required inputs, reusable-workflow inputs, and pinned-SHA comments that name the wrong version. Also flags retired runner labels (live runner-images list), script injection through ${{ github.event... }} in run:, pull_request_target checkouts of PR code, and a missing permissions key. Returns each finding with line, path, fix and doc link, per-action resolution, fix_message, and pinned_workflow: the same file with every action pinned to its full commit SHA and a # version comment (retired or missing refs move to the latest release; upgrade:true moves all). Example: {"workflow":"on: push
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node_version: 20"}. Does not run the workflow, evaluate expressions or see private repositories, secrets or repository settings. Up to 200000 characters.

workflow.description: The YAML text of a workflow file (.github/workflows/<name>.yml) or of an action.yml / action.yaml.

upgrade.description: Pin every action to its latest release instead of the version the file uses. Default false (retired or missing refs are moved to the latest release either way).

live.description: Resolve actions, inputs and runner labels on github.com. Default true; false = offline YAML and syntax checks only.

kind.description: auto (default) detects a workflow (jobs:) or an action metadata file (runs:).

tools.name: tack_resolve_actions
tools.description: Use when a uses: line for a GitHub Action is about to be written and its current version, commit SHA or inputs are needed, or the user asks what the latest version of an action is, what SHA a tag points to, or whether an action or tag exists (signals: "latest actions/checkout", "pin setup-node to a SHA", "what inputs does this action take", "does v9 exist", "which version is this SHA"). Takes owner/repo (latest release), owner/repo@ref or owner/repo/path@ref, reads the tags and branches live from github.com and the action.yml at that commit, and returns per action: exists or not, the commit SHA, the release a SHA or major tag points to, the latest release and major tag, runs.using (flags node20 and older, which GitHub stopped shipping on 2026-09-23), retired versions that fail jobs, the declared inputs, and a ready-to-paste line: uses: owner/repo@<40-char sha> # vX.Y.Z. Example: {"actions":["actions/checkout","actions/setup-node@v4","docker/build-push-action@v6"]}. Up to 30 per call. Public github.com repositories only; for a whole workflow file use tack_check_workflow.

actions.description: Action references: "owner/repo" (latest release), "owner/repo@v4", "owner/repo/path@ref", or a full uses: line.

upgrade.description: For references with a ref, return the pinned line for the latest release instead. Default false.

tools.name: sieve_test_regex
tools.description: Use when you have written, been given or are about to commit a regular expression and need to know what it really matches, instead of predicting it (signals: "write a regex for", "does this regex match", "validate emails/phone numbers/dates/slugs/URLs with a regex", "why doesn't my regex match", "test this pattern", "regex for Go", "is this regex safe", "catastrophic backtracking", "convert this Python regex to JavaScript"). Executes the pattern on the real engine: JavaScript (V8 RegExp, the engine in Chrome, Node.js and Cloudflare Workers; flags d g i m s u v y) or RE2 (re2js, with Go regexp parity: Go, RE2, Google Sheets and BigQuery syntax; flags i m s). Give strings that must match and strings that must not; each case comes back pass/fail with the matched text, index and capture groups (numbered and named), and why a "should not match" string matched (usually a missing ^...$). match: "full" tests the whole string. texts lists every match, replace_with shows the replacement ($1/$<name> in JavaScript, $1/${name} in Go). For JavaScript it also runs a ReDoS analysis (recheck): proven linear, or exponential/polynomial backtracking with a concrete attack string and the hot part of the pattern. Flags patterns that compile but mislead: ^a|b$ anchoring, \A/\Z/\h read as letters, [[:alpha:]], {,3}, [A-z], unescaped dots before extensions. Invalid patterns return the engine's error and a hint (Python (?P<name>), (?i), possessive and atomic groups; lookarounds and backreferences in RE2). Example: {"pattern":"[\\w.+-]+@[\\w-]+\\.[a-z]{2,}","should_match":["ann@example.com"],"should_not_match":["ann@example","see ann@x.io now"]}. Does not run Python, PCRE, Java or .NET engines; it reports what differs for common constructs. Up to 100 strings of 20000 characters; on a ReDoS-vulnerable pattern, long strings are skipped instead of hanging. Returns {valid, verdict: ok|warnings|redos|fails|invalid, summary, engine, engine_name, pattern, flags, match_mode, counts:{should_match, should_not_match, texts, passed, failed, skipped}, group_count, cases:[{text, length, expect: match|no_match|any, matched, pass (null = skipped), match_count, match:{text, index, end, groups?, named?}, matches? (texts only), why?, replaced?, skipped?}], warnings:[{rule, message, fix?, index?}], redos:{status: safe|vulnerable|unknown, complexity: linear|polynomial (degree n)|exponential|no attack found|unknown, attack?:{repr, length, string|null, sample}, hotspots?:[{start, end, text}], explanation?, fix_hint?, note?}|null, fix_message (ready-to-apply list, null when clean), error? and hint? (invalid patterns), notes, checked_at, open_url}.

pattern.description: The regex source, e.g. "^\\d{4}-\\d{2}$" (JSON-escaped), or a JavaScript literal "/^\\d+$/i" (flags then come from the literal).

flags.description: JavaScript: any of d g i m s u v y. RE2: i m s. Default none.

engine.description: "javascript" (default; also TypeScript, Node.js, browsers, Deno, Bun) or "re2" (Go regexp, RE2, Google Sheets REGEXMATCH, BigQuery).

should_match.description: Strings the pattern must match (in match mode).

should_not_match.description: Strings the pattern must not match.

texts.description: Strings to search; every match is listed with its groups (no pass/fail).

match.description: "search" (default): a match anywhere counts, like RegExp.test, re.search or Go MatchString. "full": the whole string must match, like Python re.fullmatch.

replace_with.description: Optional replacement; each case also returns the string with every match replaced.

max_matches.description: Most matches listed per text (default 10). match_count is always the full count.

check_redos.description: Run the ReDoS analysis (JavaScript engine). Default true.

tools.name: sieve_check_redos
tools.description: Use when a regular expression will run on user input or untrusted data (form validation, request routing, log parsing, WAF or search rules) and must not hang the server, or when reviewing a codebase's regexes for ReDoS (signals: "is this regex safe", "ReDoS", "catastrophic backtracking", "regex hangs", "CPU spike on validation", "security review of regexes", "(a+)+"). Analyzes 1 to 20 patterns with recheck (automaton analysis with a fuzzing fallback) for backtracking engines with JavaScript syntax, and returns per pattern: safe (proven linear, or no attack found when backreferences or lookarounds force fuzzing), or vulnerable with the complexity (exponential, or polynomial with its degree), a concrete attack string (repr like 'a'.repeat(31) + '\\x00', plus the string itself when short), the hot part of the pattern and a fix hint. Example: {"patterns":["^(a+)+$","/^([a-z]+\\s)*$/","^[\\w.+-]+@[\\w-]+\\.[\\w.-]+$"]}. Python re, PCRE, Java, .NET and Ruby backtrack the same way on these constructs; RE2, Go regexp and Rust regex are linear-time and not affected. To also run the pattern on test strings, use sieve_test_regex.

flags.description: Flags for every pattern given as a raw source (literals keep their own). JavaScript flags d g i m s u v y.

tools.name: ripe_check_file
tools.description: Use when a Dockerfile, docker-compose/compose.yaml, Kubernetes manifest, GitHub Actions workflow, package.json, pyproject.toml, requirements.txt, go.mod, global.json, .nvmrc, .python-version, .tool-versions, mise.toml, Gemfile, composer.json or Terraform file has just been written or edited, or the user asks whether the versions in it are current (signals: "write a Dockerfile", "FROM node:18", "python:3.9-slim", "is this base image outdated", "end of life", "EOL", "upgrade the runtime", "which Node version", "does this tag exist", "manifest unknown", "engines", "requires-python"). Reads every version pin with its line (FROM and image: references with build-arg defaults, engines/volta/packageManager, requires-python, go and toolchain directives, sdk.version, setup-* versions and matrices, and well-known frameworks such as Next.js, React, Django, Rails, Laravel), then checks each one live: support status on today's date from endoflife.date (supported, security fixes only, end of life, not released, no such version), the end-of-life date and days left, the latest patch in that line, the newest supported line and the oldest one still supported; for container images it also checks the base OS in the tag (alpine3.18, bookworm, jammy), deprecated official images, and that the tag really exists on its registry (Docker Hub, ghcr.io, mcr.microsoft.com, quay.io and others), and proposes a replacement tag that it confirmed exists. Returns findings with severity, line, message and fix, plus a fix_message. Example: {"filename":"Dockerfile","content":"FROM node:18-alpine3.18\nRUN npm ci\nFROM python:3.9-slim-buster"}. Does not build images, resolve npm or PyPI dependency trees (packages are checked only when endoflife.date tracks them), or see private registries. Up to 100000 characters.

filename.description: File name or path, used to tell the file type: "Dockerfile", "compose.yaml", ".github/workflows/ci.yml", "package.json", "pyproject.toml", "go.mod", ".nvmrc"... Optional when kind is given or the content makes it obvious.

kind.description: File type; default auto (from filename, then content).

as_of.description: Judge support status on this date (YYYY-MM-DD). Default: today (UTC).

warn_days.description: Warn when end of life is this many days away or less. Default 180.

check_tags.description: Check Docker image tags exist on their registry (and verify the suggested replacement tag). Default true.

tools.name: ripe_check_versions
tools.description: Use when a version of a runtime, framework, database, OS or Docker image is about to be chosen or recommended, or the user asks whether a version is still supported, when it reaches end of life, what the latest version or current LTS is, or whether a Docker tag exists (signals: "which Node version should I use", "latest LTS", "is Python 3.9 still supported", "when does Postgres 14 go EOL", "is .NET 8 end of life", "latest Django", "does python:3.13-slim-trixie exist", "Ubuntu 22.04 support"). Each item is free text: "node 18", "python 3.9.18", "postgres:13-alpine" (an image), "django>=4.2", "ubuntu jammy", "lts/hydrogen", or just a product name ("nodejs") for its supported lines and current pick. Data is fetched live from endoflife.date (about 490 products: languages, frameworks, databases, operating systems, cloud and infrastructure software); image tags are checked on their registry. Returns per item the matched release line, status on today's date (supported, security fixes only, end of life, not released, no such version), LTS flag, end-of-life date and days left, paid extended support date, latest patch and whether the given version is behind it, the recommended line and the oldest still supported, and for images whether the tag exists plus a verified replacement. Example: {"items":["node 18","python:3.9-slim","postgres 14","nextjs 13.4.1","dotnet"]}. Up to 40 items. Products endoflife.date does not track are reported as unknown, not guessed; for a whole file use ripe_check_file.

items.description: Products and versions, one per item: "node 18", "python 3.12.4", "postgres:16-alpine", "django 5.1", "ubuntu 22.04", "dotnet" (product only).

as_of.description: Judge support status on this date (YYYY-MM-DD). Default: today (UTC).

warn_days.description: Warn when end of life is this many days away or less. Default 180.

check_tags.description: Check Docker image tags exist on their registry (and verify the suggested replacement tag). Default true.
